title: The Long Shadow of the Iran Shock
gist: Bordoff and O'Sullivan (in an essay cut short by a paywall) note that despite the Strait of Hormuz — roughly a fifth of global oil and LNG flows — being largely closed for months in 2026, oil prices stayed low and the global economy avoided the recession past energy shocks would have produced, but warn against concluding that energy-disruption risk has been overstated.

themes.theme: A muted energy shock despite Hormuz closure

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies normally passes, has been largely closed for months as of mid-2026.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: A closure of this scale and duration at a chokepoint carrying ~20% of global oil/LNG flow would historically be expected to produce a major price spike; its absence is itself a data point worth tracking for energy-market resilience analysis.
insights.quote: The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies normally passes, has been largely closed for months.

insights.claim: Despite the prolonged Hormuz closure, oil prices have remained low, natural gas markets have proved resilient, and the global economy has so far avoided the kind of recession that many past energy shocks produced.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: Suggests global energy markets and strategic reserves have absorbed a shock that would previously have been considered catastrophic — relevant to reassessing tail-risk pricing for Middle East energy-supply disruptions.
insights.quote: Yet when considered against the nightmare scenarios contemplated at the war’s outset, oil prices have remained low and natural gas markets have proved resilient. The global economy has so far avoided the kind of recession that many past energy shocks produced.

insights.claim: The authors explicitly warn against concluding from this muted market reaction that the dangers of energy supply disruptions have been overstated, signaling the essay will argue for continued vigilance despite the apparent calm.
insights.speaker: Jason Bordoff
insights.so_what: Sets up a contrarian caution against complacency in energy-security planning even when near-term price signals look benign — relevant for scenario-planning around future Gulf disruptions.
